questions.q: What does AEIOU stand for in the AEIOU observation framework?
options: Attitudes, Emotions, Insights, Observations, Understanding
Activities, Experiences, Interactions, Objects, Users
Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects, Users
Activities, Environments, Insights, Objects, Users
questions.explain: AEIOU is a field-observation checklist with five categories: Activities (goal-directed things people do), Environments (the setting), Interactions (exchanges between people, or between people and things), Objects (the items and devices present) and Users (the people being observed). Every category is something a researcher can actually see in the field, not a feeling or a conclusion.
why_wrong: Swaps every letter for an abstract or mental word; AEIOU records observable things such as activities and objects, not attitudes, emotions or insights.
E stands for Environments, the physical setting; 'Experiences' is a common mix-up.
I stands for Interactions, the exchanges people have; 'Insights' are conclusions drawn later, not a category of observation.

questions.q: In the AEIOU framework, which category records the character of the setting itself — its layout, lighting, noise and crowding?
options: Environments
Objects
Activities
Users
questions.explain: Environments covers the whole space where the activity happens: its layout, atmosphere and function. Individual items inside that space, such as a card machine or a signboard, are recorded under Objects instead.
why_wrong: Objects are the individual items and devices within the space, not the space's layout, lighting or noise.
Activities are the goal-directed things people do, such as queuing for lunch, not features of the setting.
Users are the people being observed, who they are and what roles they have, not the place they are in.

questions.q: What is the AEIOU framework mainly used for in design thinking?
options: Generating new ideas by substituting, combining or adapting parts of an existing product
Measuring how long users take to complete a task in a usability test
Writing the final point-of-view statement for the design challenge
Organising what a researcher observes about people in a real setting
questions.explain: AEIOU is an observation tool used while empathising. It gives the researcher five headings for sorting field notes, so nothing important about the setting is missed. Defining the problem and generating ideas come later and use other tools.
why_wrong: Substituting, combining and adapting are prompts from SCAMPER, an ideation technique, not AEIOU.
Timing tasks produces quantitative usability data during testing; AEIOU sorts qualitative field observations.
The POV statement is written when defining the problem, after observations have been gathered and organised.

questions.q: What are the four quadrants of the four-quadrant empathy map used in this course?
options: Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects
Says, Thinks, Does, Feels
Think & Feel, Hear, See, Say & Do
Name, Background, Goals, Frustrations
questions.explain: The four-quadrant empathy map sorts research evidence into Says (the user's own words), Thinks (inferred thoughts and beliefs), Does (observed actions) and Feels (emotions). Putting them side by side exposes gaps and contradictions, such as between what a user says and what they do.
why_wrong: These are four of the five AEIOU observation categories, which belong to a different tool.
These are four of the six sections of the original XPLANE empathy map, which also has Pain and Gain; they are not the Says/Thinks/Does/Feels quadrants.
Name, background, goals and frustrations are typical contents of a persona, not empathy-map quadrants.

questions.q: In design thinking, what is a persona?
options: A research-based fictional archetype representing a group of users with similar goals and behaviours
A word-for-word record of what one particular interviewee said in a session
A timeline of the stages a user passes through while using a service
A real customer selected by the team to approve the final design
questions.explain: A persona is synthesised from research on many users. The team gives one archetype a name and a background so it can design for a concrete person rather than for 'everyone'. Because it is a synthesis, it does not belong to any single interviewee.
why_wrong: A persona combines many users and is not a transcript of one person; verbatim words belong in interview notes or the Says quadrant.
A timeline of stages over time is a journey map, not a persona.
A persona is not a real individual at all; it is a composite archetype built from research.

questions.q: Which tool lays out the sequence of stages a user goes through over time, with their actions and feelings at each stage?
options: Empathy map
Persona
Journey map
Affinity diagram
questions.explain: A journey map is organised along time. It follows the user from stage to stage and records what they do and feel at each one, which shows where the experience breaks down. An empathy map is a snapshot with no time axis.
why_wrong: An empathy map sorts evidence into Says, Thinks, Does and Feels; it has no sequence of stages over time.
A persona describes who a representative user is, not the steps of their experience.
An affinity diagram groups research notes into themes by similarity, not into a time sequence.

questions.q: Qualitative user research is mainly concerned with which of these?
options: How many users completed the task
What percentage of users prefer design A
The average time users take to finish a task
Why users behave as they do, described through their words and actions
questions.explain: Qualitative research is descriptive: interviews and observation show why people act as they do. Counts, percentages and task times measure how many or how much, so they are quantitative.
why_wrong: 'How many' is a count, which makes it quantitative.
A percentage is a measured number, which makes it quantitative.
A task time is a measurement, which makes it quantitative.

questions.q: In a user interview, what is an open question?
options: A question worded so that it hints at the answer the interviewer expects
A question that invites a full answer in the participant's own words, not just yes or no
A question that the participant can fully answer with a simple yes or no
A question that asks the participant to rate something on a scale of 1 to 5
questions.explain: Open questions, which often begin with 'how', 'what' or 'tell me about', let participants describe their experience freely. This brings out details the researcher did not think to ask about. Yes/no and rating questions limit the answer to options the researcher already chose.
why_wrong: That describes a leading question, which pushes the participant towards an answer.
That describes a closed question.
A rating question fixes the answer to a number on a scale, so it is closed, not open.

questions.q: A behaviour-anchored interview question asks the participant about what?
options: A specific real occasion in the past, such as the last time they did the task
What they would do in an imagined future situation
Whether they agree with the interviewer's own idea
How they would rate the product on a numbered scale
questions.explain: A behaviour-anchored question ties the answer to something that actually happened, for example 'Tell me about the last time you looked for a room in a block you had never visited.' People describe real past events more accurately than they predict their own future behaviour or give general opinions.
why_wrong: That is a hypothetical question: it asks for a prediction, not a real past behaviour.
Asking for agreement with the interviewer's idea makes the question leading.
A rating scale produces a number, not an account of a real occasion.

questions.q: What is an explicit user need?
options: A need the researcher infers from the user's behaviour or workarounds
A need that has been confirmed by counting how many users share it
A need the user states directly, in their own words
A need that is always phrased as a specific feature
questions.explain: Explicit needs are the ones users say out loud, for example in an interview. What decides the label is how the need was found (stated by the user), not how many people share it or how it is worded.
why_wrong: A need inferred from behaviour or workarounds is an implicit need.
Counting users is quantitative evidence of how common a need is; it does not show whether the need was stated.
An explicit need can be worded in any way; users often voice solutions, but the label comes from the need being stated, not from its wording.

questions.q: An implicit user need is identified mainly from which of these?
options: The user's direct answer when asked, 'What do you need?'
The user's behaviour, contradictions between what they say and do, and workarounds they have built
The list of features in a competitor's product
The design team's own brainstormed solution ideas
questions.explain: Implicit needs are never voiced, so they have to be inferred from evidence such as a repeated behaviour, a gap between what someone says and what they do, or a workaround they have created. That is why observation matters as much as asking questions.
why_wrong: A need given in the user's own answer is stated, so it is explicit.
A competitor's features describe another product, not what your users need.
Brainstormed solutions come from the team during ideation; they are ideas, not evidence of a user need.

questions.q: Which of these is the standard point-of-view (POV) statement template?
options: How might we [action] for [user]?
[User] wants [feature] so that [benefit].
[Product] helps [user] by [feature].
[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight].
questions.explain: A POV statement has three parts: a specific user, a need written as an outcome, and an insight from research that explains why the need matters. It defines the problem. How Might We questions are built from it afterwards to start ideation.
why_wrong: That is a How Might We question, which turns the POV into an opportunity for ideation.
This template puts a feature where the need should be and contains no research insight.
That describes a product and its feature, which makes it a solution statement rather than a problem definition.

questions.q: In a point-of-view statement, what goes after the word 'because'?
options: An insight about the user, drawn from research
The feature the team plans to build
The user's name and age
The number of users who were interviewed
questions.explain: The 'because' clause carries the insight: the research finding that explains why the user has this need. Without it, the statement names a need but does not tell the team what drives it.
why_wrong: A feature is a solution, and putting one in the POV closes off other ideas before ideation starts.
Name and age are persona details; they identify the user but do not explain the need.
A count of interviews describes the research sample, not an insight about the user.

questions.q: How should the need in a problem statement be phrased?
options: As a specific feature, such as 'needs a green confirmation button'
As the technology the team will use, such as 'needs a mobile app'
As an outcome the user wants, such as 'needs to know the payment went through'
As the team's business goal, such as 'needs more app downloads'
questions.explain: A need written as an outcome describes what the user wants to achieve and leaves every possible solution open. Writing a feature into the need turns the problem statement into a solution statement and narrows ideation before it has started.
why_wrong: A confirmation button is one possible solution; the need behind it is knowing the payment succeeded.
A mobile app is a technology choice, which is a solution and not the user's need.
More downloads is the business's goal, not something the user needs.

questions.q: A researcher's field notes from a campus canteen read: (1) Students are queuing to collect lunch. (2) The hall is noisy, crowded and poorly lit. (3) There is one card-swipe machine and a tray of printed token slips. (4) A student asks the cashier whether the thali is still available. Which AEIOU categories do notes 1–4 belong to?
options: 1 Activities, 2 Objects, 3 Environments, 4 Interactions
1 Activities, 2 Environments, 3 Objects, 4 Interactions
1 Interactions, 2 Environments, 3 Objects, 4 Activities
1 Users, 2 Environments, 3 Objects, 4 Interactions
questions.explain: Queuing for lunch is a goal-directed thing people do (Activities). Noise, crowding and lighting describe the setting (Environments), and the card machine and token slips are items within it (Objects). A student asking the cashier a question is an exchange between two people (Interactions).
why_wrong: Swaps the setting and the items: noise and lighting describe the Environment, while the machine and slips are Objects.
Swaps notes 1 and 4: queuing is the Activity, and the question to the cashier is the Interaction that happens within it.
Note 1 records what the students are doing, not who they are, so it is an Activity rather than Users.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five AEIOU observation categories?
options: Interactions
Environments
Users
Insights
questions.explain: The five AEIOU categories are Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects and Users. The I stands for Interactions, meaning exchanges between people or between people and things. Insights are conclusions the team draws later from the observations; they are not recorded in the field.
why_wrong: Interactions is the genuine I of AEIOU; picking it comes from assuming the I stands for Insights.
Environments is the genuine E of AEIOU; picking it comes from assuming the E stands for Emotions or Experiences.
Users is the genuine U of AEIOU; picking it comes from assuming the U stands for Understanding.

questions.q: What does a persona contain that a four-quadrant empathy map (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels) does not?
options: A name, background and goals presented as one archetype standing for a whole group of similar users
Separate records of what the user says, thinks, does and feels
The stages of the user's experience in time order, with the user's feelings at each stage
A ranked list of solution ideas that the team plans to prototype next
questions.explain: An empathy map sorts evidence into four quadrants but does not turn it into a character. A persona goes further: it combines research on many users into one named archetype with a background, goals and frustrations that the team can design for.
why_wrong: Says, Thinks, Does and Feels are the empathy map's own quadrants, so this is something the empathy map already has.
Stages in time order belong to a journey map, which is neither a persona nor an empathy map.
Solution ideas come from ideation; neither a persona nor an empathy map is a list of solutions.

questions.q: On a four-quadrant empathy map (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels), where do these three pieces of evidence go? (a) a direct quotation from the participant; (b) an action the researcher watched the participant perform; (c) the researcher's cautious inference about what the participant believes.
options: (a) Says, (b) Says, (c) Does
(a) Thinks, (b) Does, (c) Says
(a) Says, (b) Does, (c) Thinks
(a) Says, (b) Does, (c) Does
questions.explain: Evidence is placed by its type, not its topic. Words the participant spoke go under Says, actions that were observed go under Does, and a cautious inference about their beliefs goes under Thinks. Keeping inferences out of Does stops the team treating a guess as something it actually saw.
why_wrong: Files the observed action under Says just because the researcher wrote it down in words, and moves the inference into Does as if it had been observed.
Swaps (a) and (c): a direct quotation is what the participant said, and an inference was never spoken, so it cannot go under Says.
Treats the inference as an observed action; nobody saw the participant's belief, so it belongs under Thinks.

questions.q: Which of these statements about empathy maps, personas and journey maps is NOT correct?
options: A persona is a synthesised archetype built from research on many users.
An empathy map lays out a user's experience as a sequence of stages over time.
A journey map follows the user through stages, recording actions and feelings at each one.
The four-quadrant empathy map sorts evidence into Says, Thinks, Does and Feels.
questions.explain: A sequence of stages over time is what defines a journey map. An empathy map has no time axis: it sorts evidence about a user into Says, Thinks, Does and Feels. The two are easily confused because both record feelings.
why_wrong: This statement is true: a persona is a synthesised archetype, not one real interviewee, so it is not the incorrect one.
This statement is true: stages over time with actions and feelings is exactly what a journey map shows.
This statement is true: these are the four quadrants of the empathy map taught in this course.

questions.q: Which of these research findings is quantitative?
options: Participants described the signboards as confusing.
One participant said she felt embarrassed asking a guard for directions.
Several participants explained that they follow classmates instead of reading the signs.
In a test, 7 of 10 participants could not find the room within five minutes.
questions.explain: Quantitative findings are counted or measured: how many, what percentage, how long. '7 of 10 within five minutes' is a count against a time limit, so it is quantitative. The other findings describe what people said, felt or did and why, which makes them qualitative.
why_wrong: A description of how participants saw the signs is descriptive, so it is qualitative.
One person's reported feeling is descriptive interview evidence, so it is qualitative.
'Several' loosely describes a behaviour and the reason for it; it is not a measured count, so this finding is qualitative.

questions.q: Which of these interview questions is a leading question?
options: Don't you find the signboards in this building confusing?
How do you usually find a classroom you have never been to before?
Tell me about the last time you had to find a room in a block you had never visited.
What do you do when you need to find a room in a new block?
questions.explain: A leading question builds the expected answer into the question (here, 'confusing') and invites the participant to agree. Neutral questions let participants describe their own experience, whether or not it matches what the researcher assumes.
why_wrong: This is an open question: it asks how, and it does not suggest any particular answer.
This is a behaviour-anchored question about a real past occasion; it assumes nothing about how the participant felt.
This is an open question about what the participant does; it does not suggest an answer.

questions.q: Which of these points to an implicit need rather than an explicit one?
options: A student says in the interview, "The room numbers on the doors should be bigger."
A student tells the interviewer, "I really wish there were more signboards in the corridors."
A student photographs the floor plan beside the lift and checks the photo at every turn, but never mentions doing so.
A student writes "please add a campus map app" in the end-of-term feedback form.
questions.explain: An implicit need is inferred from behaviour or a workaround; the user does not state it. Photographing the floor plan is a workaround the student created and never mentioned, so it reveals an unspoken need: a way to keep track of where she is in the building. The other three are stated requests, so they are explicit.
why_wrong: The student said this out loud, so it is explicit, and it is also phrased as a solution.
A wish voiced to the interviewer is stated, so it is explicit.
Writing a request in a feedback form is still stating it, so it is explicit.

questions.q: Which of these user comments describes a pain point rather than a request for a particular solution?
options: You should build an app with indoor GPS.
I only find out a room is on the upper floor after I've climbed the wrong staircase.
Put colour-coded arrows on the floor.
I want a touchscreen kiosk at the entrance.
questions.explain: A pain point describes the friction the user experiences, while a solution request names a fix the user has already imagined. The staircase comment tells the team what goes wrong and leaves them free to explore many fixes. Each of the others commits to one feature.
why_wrong: An indoor GPS app is a solution the user proposes, not the friction itself.
Floor arrows are one specific fix, so this is a solution request.
A kiosk is one specific fix; the comment says what the user wants built, not what goes wrong.

questions.q: Which of these is correctly classified?
options: A student says, "I wish the portal loaded faster" — implicit need.
A student never complains about waking up, but sets five backup alarms before every exam — explicit need.
A need the researcher inferred from a user's workaround — explicit, because the researcher wrote it down.
A student says the canteen queue is fine, yet leaves it every day to eat outside — implicit need.
questions.explain: Explicit needs are stated by the user; implicit needs are inferred from behaviour, a contradiction or a workaround. In the canteen case, what the student says contradicts what she does, so the need it points to is implicit. Who writes a need down does not change its type.
why_wrong: The student said it out loud, so the need is explicit, not implicit.
Nothing was said; the need is inferred from a repeated workaround, so it is implicit, not explicit.
Writing a need down does not make it explicit; it was inferred rather than stated by the user, so it is implicit.

questions.q: Which of these is a complete, well-formed point-of-view statement?
options: A first-year student visiting a new block needs a way to reach her classroom on time because the signs use building codes she has not learned yet.
A first-year student visiting a new block needs a campus navigation app because the signs are confusing.
A first-year student visiting a new block needs a way to reach her classroom on time.
Students on this campus need better signage because the signs are confusing.
questions.explain: A POV needs three parts: a specific user, a need phrased as an outcome, and a research insight after 'because'. Only the first statement has all three. Its insight, that the signs use building codes she has not learned, tells the team why the need exists.
why_wrong: Puts a feature (a navigation app) where the need should be, which turns the POV into a solution statement.
Has a user and a need but no 'because' insight, so the team does not know why the need exists.
The user is vague, 'better signage' is a solution rather than a need, and 'the signs are confusing' repeats the complaint instead of explaining it.

questions.q: Arrange these steps in the order a team would normally follow. P: Write a point-of-view statement. Q: Observe and interview users. R: Sort the evidence onto an empathy map. S: Identify the users' needs from the map.
options: Q → S → R → P
P → Q → R → S
Q → R → S → P
R → Q → S → P
questions.explain: Evidence comes first, so observation and interviews start the sequence. Next the evidence is sorted onto the empathy map and the needs are read from the map. The POV is written last because it states a need and an insight that the earlier steps produced.
why_wrong: Identifies needs before sorting the evidence, but step S reads the needs from the map, so R has to come before S.
Writes the POV before any research, yet a POV has to rest on needs and insights found in the field.
Builds the empathy map before observing anyone, so there would be no evidence to put on it.

questions.q: Your team is sent to watch the hostel mess during dinner for one hour. You may not interview anyone. The mentor wants the notes organised so that nothing about the scene is missed: who is there, what they do, how they deal with each other and with things, the space itself, and the things in it. Which tool should structure your notes?
options: A four-quadrant empathy map (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels) of the mess
A persona of the typical student who eats at the mess
An AEIOU sheet with headings for Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects and Users
A point-of-view statement written before entering the mess
questions.explain: AEIOU is an observation framework. Its five headings make the observer record what people do (Activities), the space (Environments), their exchanges with people and things (Interactions), the things themselves (Objects) and who the people are (Users). It is used while watching a setting, which is exactly this brief. Empathy maps and personas are built afterwards to make sense of what was learned about users, and a POV comes later still.
why_wrong: An empathy map is organised around one user's words, actions, thoughts and feelings, not around a whole scene. It has no heading for the space or the things in it.
A persona is an archetype pieced together after research across many users. It cannot structure raw notes while you are still observing.
A POV defines the problem after research. Writing one before observing puts the conclusion ahead of the evidence.

questions.q: During an AEIOU observation at the library photocopy counter, a teammate writes under Activities: 'Students are careless and waste time in the queue.' Which rewrite turns this into a usable observation note?
options: Students are impatient in the queue and do not plan their printing in advance.
Students wait in a queue of about eight; most look at their phones, and two leave before reaching the counter.
Students need an online print-order system so that they never have to queue.
Students feel the queue system at the counter is unfair to them.
questions.explain: An observation note records what could be seen or heard: who did what, how many, for how long. Judgement is left for later, when the notes are analysed. The correct rewrite describes behaviour that anyone standing at the counter could confirm. 'Careless', 'impatient' and 'feel … unfair' are the observer's interpretations, and an online system is a solution, not an observation.
why_wrong: 'Impatient' and 'do not plan' are still judgements about the students, not something the observer saw. It is the original mistake in politer words.
It names a solution. An observation note records what happens, and jumping to a fix skips the research the note is meant to feed.
It states the students' feelings as fact although nobody said so. That is an inference, not an observed activity.

questions.q: An observer at the library entrance notes: 'A student taps her ID card on the gate reader three times; it beeps red twice before the gate opens.' A teammate says this cannot go under Interactions because no second person is involved, so it must go under Objects. Which response is correct?
options: The teammate is right: Interactions covers only exchanges between two or more people, so a person using a machine is recorded under Objects.
It belongs under Environments, because the gate reader is part of the entrance and Environments covers the fixtures of the space.
It belongs under Users, because it records how one particular student behaved at the entrance.
It belongs under Interactions, because that category covers a person's exchanges with someone or something else, machines included; the reader itself is listed under Objects.
questions.explain: In AEIOU, Interactions are exchanges between a person and someone or something else. A person–machine exchange such as tapping a card and getting a beep therefore counts. The reader as a thing (what it is and where it sits) goes under Objects, but the back-and-forth of taps and beeps is an interaction. Interactions are the building blocks of activities; here the larger activity is entering the library.
why_wrong: This narrows Interactions to exchanges between people. The category explicitly includes a person's exchanges with objects and machines.
Environments records the character of the setting (layout, lighting, noise, crowding), not one person's exchange with a single device.
Users records who the people are, such as their roles and relationships, not the step-by-step exchange one person had with a device.

questions.q: After an AEIOU observation at a bus stop, a teammate proposes: 'U stands for Understanding, so let us write our conclusions about why the crowd forms under U.' Which correction is right?
options: U stands for Users, meaning the people observed and their roles. Conclusions are not an AEIOU category; they are drawn out later, when the notes are analysed.
The teammate is right: U holds the team's understanding of the scene, which is why it comes last in the sequence.
U stands for Users, but conclusions belong under I, which stands for Insights drawn from the other four headings.
U stands for Users, but conclusions belong under O, which stands for Observations the team has interpreted.
questions.explain: AEIOU stands for Activities, Environments, Interactions, Objects and Users: five categories, all of them things an observer can see. 'I' is Interactions and 'O' is Objects, so there is no slot for conclusions. Explanations of why something happens come afterwards, when the team groups its notes and looks for patterns. Keeping them out of the notes stops guesses being mistaken for evidence.
why_wrong: U is Users, not Understanding. AEIOU records what is observed, not the observer's conclusions.
I stands for Interactions, not Insights. Insights come from analysing the notes after observing, not from an AEIOU heading.
O stands for Objects, not Observations. Every AEIOU heading is already a kind of observation.

questions.q: On one student's empathy map, the Says quadrant holds 'I always check the notice board for exam updates'. The Does quadrant records that over three days of observation she never looked at the board and instead asked classmates in the class group chat. What should the team do with these two entries?
options: Delete the Says entry, because observed behaviour is more reliable than what people say.
Move the quotation to Does, since it describes her behaviour.
Keep both entries, because the gap between what she says and what she does is a clue worth following up for an insight.
Merge them into a single note under Feels, such as 'feels unsure about exam updates'.
questions.explain: An empathy map is meant to hold contradictions side by side, because the real insight often lies in the gap between Says and Does. Perhaps she trusts classmates more than the board, or the board is hard to use. Deleting either entry throws away evidence. Moving the quote misfiles it: words the participant spoke always go under Says, whatever they are about.
why_wrong: Deleting the quote loses the contradiction itself, which is the most useful clue on the map.
Quadrants are chosen by type of evidence, not by topic. Words she spoke stay under Says even when they describe her behaviour.
Merging two pieces of evidence into an invented feeling destroys both. Feels should hold emotions the evidence supports, not a compromise between entries.

questions.q: A team's persona draft for 'Aman, 18, first-year day scholar' contains these four lines. Which one should be taken out of the persona?
options: Goal: reach his 9 a.m. class without running from the bus stop.
Frustration: the college bus timetable changes without notice.
Behaviour: leaves home 40 minutes early 'just in case'.
Planned feature: a live bus-tracking app with push alerts.
questions.explain: A persona describes the user through goals, behaviours, needs and frustrations drawn from research, so the team can judge ideas against him later. A planned feature is the team's own solution, not a fact about Aman. Writing it into the persona builds an answer into the tool that is meant to test answers. Features belong in ideation, after the problem has been defined.
why_wrong: Goals are core persona content: they state what the user is trying to achieve.
Frustrations are core persona content and feed directly into the problem definition.
Observed behaviours, including workarounds like leaving early, are what make a persona research-based.

questions.q: A team builds a persona called 'Riya, 19, hosteller' by copying the name, exact quotes and daily routine of their most articulate interviewee, whose real name is Riya. The mentor objects. Which statement identifies the actual problem?
options: A persona must never include a name or a quotation, so both should be removed from the draft.
A persona is an archetype built from patterns across many users. This one records a single interviewee, who may be unusual.
Nothing is wrong: a persona is supposed to record what one specific interviewee said and did.
Personas hold only demographic facts such as age and course, so the quotes and routine belong on an empathy map.
questions.explain: A persona is a behavioural archetype built from patterns seen across many participants. It usually gets a name, a representative quote and details so it feels real, but it is not any one person. Copying one interviewee produces a portrait of that single individual, which is what an empathy map of that participant would record, and the team may end up designing for an outlier. The fix is to rebuild the persona from what the interviews have in common.
why_wrong: Personas usually do carry a name and a representative quote so they feel real. The problem is where the content came from, not that it exists.
This is the trap. Recording one specific interviewee is what an empathy map of that person does; a persona is built up across many users.
Personas hold goals, behaviours, needs and frustrations, not just demographics. The quotes and routine are not the problem; the fact that they come from one person is.

questions.q: A researcher watched a student walk past the photocopier queue straight to the counter, then go back and join the end of the queue after the attendant pointed at it. She never spoke. Under Does, the researcher wrote: 'Walked straight to the counter because she thought the queue was only for staff.' How should this entry be handled on a four-quadrant empathy map?
options: Keep the whole sentence under Does, because it is a single account of what she did at the counter.
Move the whole sentence to Says, because the researcher recorded it in words during the session.
Split it. The walk to the counter and the return to the queue go under Does, and 'thought the queue was only for staff' goes under Thinks as a tentative inference.
Delete the 'because' part, since an empathy map should record only what was directly seen or heard.
questions.explain: Each piece of evidence is filed by its type. The walk to the counter and the return to the queue were observed, so they go under Does. The reason was never spoken or seen; it is the researcher's guess about what she believed, so it goes under Thinks, marked as tentative. Inferences are not banned: Thinks exists for exactly these cautious guesses, as long as they are not presented as observations.
why_wrong: Leaving the inference under Does presents a guess as if it had been observed. That is the misfiling the quadrants exist to prevent.
Says holds the participant's own words. She said nothing, and the researcher writing a note does not turn it into a quotation.
The Thinks quadrant exists for cautious inferences about what the user believes. Deleting this one throws away a useful lead.

questions.q: A teammate drafts this interview question for first-year students: 'Wouldn't a big map at the block entrance help you find your classrooms faster?' Which rewrite fixes its problems?
options: Tell me about the last time you had to find a classroom you had never been to. What did you do?
Would you use a map at the entrance if we put one up there next term?
Don't you think finding classrooms in this block is really confusing?
On a scale of 1 to 5, how useful would a map at the entrance be for you?
questions.explain: The draft has three problems: it is leading (it signals the answer 'yes'), it is closed, and it is built around the team's own solution. The rewrite is open, neutral and tied to a real past event, so the student describes what actually happened instead of guessing about a future product. Questions about real past behaviour produce evidence; hypothetical questions about features mostly produce polite agreement.
why_wrong: It still centres on the team's own solution and asks for a yes-or-no guess about the future instead of a description of real behaviour.
It swaps one leading question for another: 'Don't you think… really confusing?' signals the answer the interviewer wants.
A rating still centres on the map idea and turns the interview into a survey item. It reveals nothing about what students actually do.

questions.q: A campus survey shows that 38 of 50 day scholars reach their first lecture late at least once a week. The team does not yet know why. Which next step fits best?
options: Send the same survey to 500 more students to make the figure more reliable.
Interview a few late-arriving students and shadow them through a morning to learn why it happens.
Write the POV now: 'Day scholars need to arrive on time because 76% are late.'
Brainstorm solutions such as extra buses, since the problem is already clear.
questions.explain: The survey is quantitative: it counts how many are late (38/50 = 76%) but cannot say why. Qualitative methods, such as interviewing and observing a few people in depth, are the tool for finding out why. A bigger sample only makes the same count more precise. Writing a POV or brainstorming now would build on a cause nobody has found.
why_wrong: More respondents make the 'how many' figure more precise but still give no reasons. The gap is qualitative, not a sample-size problem.
A statistic is not an insight. The 'because' clause must explain why the need exists, and the team does not know that yet.
Jumping to solutions assumes the cause (not enough buses) before any research has found it.

questions.q: In six interviews, hostellers complained that the mess runs out of breakfast by 8:15 a.m. Before changing anything, the team wants to know whether most of the 2,000 hostellers face this, or only these six. Which method fits this question?
options: More one-hour in-depth interviews with other hostellers until the pattern feels clear
A persona built from the six interviewees' answers about breakfast
An empathy map for each of the six interviewees, compared side by side
A short survey of a large sample of hostellers, asking when they reach the mess and how often breakfast has run out
questions.explain: 'How many' and 'how widespread' are quantitative questions, so a survey of a large sample is the method that fits. The interviews found the issue and explain why it matters; the survey checks how far it extends. Personas and empathy maps organise evidence the team already has and cannot show how common something is.
why_wrong: In-depth interviews are the qualitative tool for finding out why. They cannot reach enough of 2,000 people to answer 'how many'.
A persona pulls existing research together into an archetype. It adds no evidence about how common the complaint is.
Empathy maps organise what the six said and did. They still describe only those six people.

questions.q: In interviews, nearly every student insists, 'I always take the stairs if I'm only going up one or two floors.' The team suspects this is not what actually happens. Which method would best settle the question?
options: A survey of 300 students asking how often they take the lift for just one or two floors
A focus group in which students discuss their lift and stair habits with one another
Watching the lift lobby at class-change times and recording how many people ride it for only one or two floors
Re-interviewing the same students and asking them to be completely honest this time
questions.explain: The doubt is about the gap between what people say and what they do. Every self-report method (survey, focus group, re-interview) just asks people to say it again. Only direct observation records actual behaviour. The survey is tempting because it is bigger, but a larger sample of the same self-report reproduces the same gap.
why_wrong: A survey is still self-report. More respondents make the stated answer more precise, not closer to real behaviour.
A focus group is self-report in a group, where people may also echo one another. It cannot show what they actually do.
Asking the same people again, however politely, still collects what they say rather than what they do.

questions.q: Which of these interview questions is both open and not leading?
options: How annoying is the hostel Wi-Fi when you study at night?
Do you find the hostel Wi-Fi annoying when you study at night?
Would you prefer a faster Wi-Fi plan or more routers on your floor?
Tell me about the last time you studied online in your room at night.
questions.explain: An open question lets the participant answer in their own words; a leading one plants the answer. 'How annoying is…' starts like an open question but assumes the Wi-Fi is annoying, so the participant can only choose how much. 'Tell me about the last time…' is open, assumes nothing, and ties the answer to a real past event.
why_wrong: It sounds open because it starts with 'How', but it assumes annoyance. The participant can only say how much, not whether.
It is closed (yes or no) and names the feeling the interviewer expects.
It is a closed either-or choice between the team's own solutions, so the participant cannot describe what actually happens.

questions.q: Asked about the college app, a student says, 'The timetable section is fine.' Over a week, the researcher sees her take a screenshot of the timetable every morning and check the screenshot, not the app, before each class. She never mentions this. Which reading of the evidence is correct?
options: It is a workaround pointing to an implicit need: quick, reliable access to her timetable.
No need should be recorded, because she said herself that the timetable section is fine.
It is an explicit need, because she repeats the screenshot habit every single day.
It points to an implicit need for a screenshot button inside the timetable section.
questions.explain: An implicit need is inferred from behaviour, a contradiction or a workaround, not from what the user says. Here all three line up: she calls the section fine, yet does extra work every day to avoid opening it. The need is written as an outcome (quick, reliable access to her timetable), not as the feature that happens to match her workaround.
why_wrong: This takes the spoken 'fine' at face value and ignores a daily workaround that contradicts it.
Explicit means stated by the user. Repeating a behaviour does not make it stated, and she never mentioned it.
It turns the need into a feature. A screenshot button is one possible solution, and naming it rules out every other.

questions.q: During a shadowing session that starts at 6:30 a.m., the researcher hears a hosteller's phone ring five times, two minutes apart, before she gets up. She set all five alarms herself. In her interview she never mentions waking up as a problem. Which is the best statement of the implicit need this suggests?
options: She needs a louder alarm app.
She needs a way to be confident she will wake up in time.
She needs to go to bed earlier.
She needs to set five alarms every morning.
questions.explain: A workaround shows the user doing extra work to protect something that matters, so ask what it gives her. Five alarms give her confidence that she will not oversleep, and the need is written as that outcome. A louder app is one solution, 'go to bed earlier' is the researcher's advice, and restating the workaround describes the behaviour, not the need behind it.
why_wrong: It names one solution. A louder alarm is only one of many ways the outcome could be met.
This is the researcher's advice about her habits, not a need inferred from what the workaround does for her.
This restates the workaround itself. The need is what the five alarms are for, not the alarms.

questions.q: In an interview, a canteen customer says, 'You need a louder bell so I know when my order is ready.' Which statement about this comment is correct?
options: It is an implicit need, because the real need behind the bell has to be dug out by the researcher.
It is explicit because she stated it, but it is phrased as a solution; the need to record is knowing when her order is ready.
It is an explicit need, and it should go into the POV exactly as stated: she needs a louder bell.
It should be set aside, because users are not designers and their suggested fixes carry little information.
questions.explain: Explicit versus implicit depends on whether the user said it. She did, and she even named the outcome herself: 'so I know when my order is ready'. But her request is a solution, and a problem definition needs the outcome behind it so the team can consider other ways to meet it, such as a token display or a message. Her suggestion is useful evidence of the pain point, not a specification to copy.
why_wrong: She said it aloud, outcome included, so it is explicit. Having to rephrase a stated request does not make it implicit.
It is explicit, but copying a feature into the POV rules out every other solution. The need must be written as an outcome.
User suggestions point straight at a real pain point. The fix is to reframe the suggestion as an outcome, not to throw it away.

questions.q: In an interview, a hosteller says, 'I don't trust the mess-card balance shown in the app, so after every meal I write my balance in my diary.' A teammate records this as an implicit need, reasoning that a workaround always signals an implicit need. Which judgement is correct?
options: It is explicit. She stated the workaround and its reason herself, so nothing was inferred: she needs to be sure her balance is right.
The teammate is right: any need that shows up through a workaround is implicit by definition.
It is implicit, because she described a habit and never actually used the word 'need'.
It is not a need at all, because writing in a diary is simply a personal habit of hers.
questions.explain: Explicit versus implicit depends on one condition: did the user state it, or did the team have to infer it? Workarounds usually reveal implicit needs because users rarely mention them. She described this one and its reason herself, so the need (to be sure her balance is correct) is explicit. If the team had only spotted the diary without her explanation, the same need would have been implicit.
why_wrong: Workarounds usually point to implicit needs only because users rarely explain them. Once she states the reason herself, nothing is inferred, so the need is explicit.
A need does not have to contain the word 'need'. She clearly stated what she lacks: trust in the balance.
A habit that costs her extra work after every meal is exactly the kind of evidence that reveals a need. Dismissing it loses the finding.

questions.q: Research summary: hostellers often walk about 10 minutes from their block to the mess, find out only at the counter that the dish is one they dislike, and then pay extra to eat outside. Several said this happens a few times a week. Which point-of-view statement best captures this research?
options: A hosteller needs a menu-display app in the hostel lobby because she dislikes some of the dishes the mess serves.
A hosteller needs a way to eat healthier food because mess food is unhealthy and she worries about her diet.
A hosteller needs a way to know what the mess is serving before she sets out, because she only finds out at the counter, after a 10-minute walk, and then pays extra to eat outside.
A hosteller needs a way to know what the mess is serving before she sets out, because she needs to know the menu in advance.
questions.explain: A POV follows '[user] needs a way to [need] because [insight]', and both the need and the insight must come from the research. The correct statement names an outcome (knowing the menu before setting out) and an insight that explains why it matters (a wasted walk and extra spending). The others put a solution where the need should be, bring in a claim the research never made, or repeat the need as its own reason.
why_wrong: It puts a solution (an app) where the need should be, and 'dislikes some dishes' misses the real cost the research found: the wasted walk and the extra spending.
Healthier food and unhealthy mess food were never part of the findings. The POV must come from the research, not from the team's assumptions.
The 'because' clause just restates the need, so it explains nothing. The insight must say why the need exists.

questions.q: A student asks for 'a dark mode in the college app'. When the researcher asks when she would use it, she explains that she revises in bed after lights-out and the bright screen wakes her roommate. What should the team carry into its problem definition?
options: The request itself: she needs a dark mode.
The pain point: she needs a way to revise at night without disturbing her sleeping roommate.
Nothing yet, because a feature request is not research evidence.
A broad need: students need a better app.
questions.explain: 'Dark mode' is a request for a particular solution. The follow-up question uncovered the pain point behind it: revising after lights-out without waking her roommate. A problem definition carries the pain point, phrased as an outcome, because that leaves room for other answers (a dimmer reading view, audio notes, a late-night study room) that a copied feature request would rule out.
why_wrong: It copies the user's proposed solution, so any POV built on it can only lead to dark mode.
The request is useful evidence: it led the researcher to the real pain point. It needs reframing, not discarding.
It is so vague that it throws away the specific user, situation and pain point the follow-up question uncovered.

questions.q: A team writes: 'A day scholar who drives to campus needs a way to book a parking slot through an app because by 9 a.m. every lot near her block is full and she circles for up to 20 minutes, missing the start of her first class.' What is the main flaw?
options: There is no flaw: it follows the 'needs a way to' template and ends with a concrete, research-based insight.
The insight contains numbers such as '9 a.m.' and '20 minutes', and a POV must stay qualitative.
The user is too specific. A POV should speak for all students, not for one day scholar who drives.
The need names a solution (booking a slot through an app) instead of an outcome such as being parked and in class on time.
questions.explain: The words 'needs a way to' do not make what follows a need. 'Book a parking slot through an app' is a feature, so the statement slips a solution into the problem. Rewritten as an outcome (being parked and in class on time), it leaves room for other ideas such as shuttles or staggered timings. The specific user and the concrete, research-based insight are strengths, not flaws.
why_wrong: The template is satisfied only on the surface. What follows 'needs a way to' is a feature, so the need is a solution in disguise.
Concrete details from research, including counts and times, strengthen an insight. Nothing forbids numbers in a POV.
A specific user is what makes a POV useful. 'All students' would make the need too vague to design for.

questions.q: A hosteller says, 'We need more washing machines. On Sunday evening, the only time I'm free, every one is taken.' Over a week, the team sees the machines standing mostly idle on weekday mornings and afternoons, and fully in use only on Sunday evenings. Which point-of-view statement best reflects the research?
options: A hosteller free only on Sunday evenings needs a way to wash then without a long wait, because demand piles into that one evening while the machines stand mostly idle on weekday mornings and afternoons.
A hosteller needs more washing machines, because on Sunday evenings every machine in the hostel is taken.
A hosteller needs a laundry booking app, because the machines stand idle on weekday mornings and afternoons.
The team cannot write a POV yet, because what the user said and what the team observed contradict each other.
questions.explain: Her request for more machines is explicit, but it is a solution, and the observation undercuts it. There are not too few machines overall; everyone wants them at the same time. A good POV keeps her real need (washing on the one evening she is free without a long wait) and uses the observed pattern as the insight. A contradiction like this is raw material for insight, not a reason to stop.
why_wrong: It copies her stated solution as the need. The observation shows the machines sit idle most of the week, so more machines is one possible fix, not the need.
It puts a solution (a booking app) where the need should be, and its 'because' clause states a fact without explaining her problem.
A gap between what users say and what is observed is where insight comes from. It calls for a sharper POV, not a delay.

questions.q: How does the unit define empathy in Design Thinking?
options: Understanding a person's feelings, experiences, motivations, frustrations and goals by seeing the world from their point of view
Feeling sorry for a person from a distance
Deciding to act to relieve a person's problem
Predicting what a person will buy next
questions.explain: Empathy means understanding what users think, feel, say and do, from the user's point of view. Feeling sorry from a distance is sympathy, and empathy plus the decision to act is compassion.
why_wrong: That is sympathy in the unit's table.
That is compassion, which adds the decision to act.
Predicting purchases is not what the unit means by empathy.

questions.q: In the unit's table, which pairing of term and meaning is correct?
options: Sympathy is understanding a situation as they experience it, and compassion is feeling for someone from a distance
Sympathy is feeling for someone from a distance, and compassion is empathy plus the decision to act
Empathy is feeling for someone from a distance, and sympathy is empathy plus the decision to act
Compassion is feeling for someone from a distance, and empathy is the decision to act
questions.explain: The unit's three words differ in distance and in whether they lead to action: sympathy feels for someone at a distance, empathy understands as they experience it, and compassion adds the decision to act.
why_wrong: This swaps sympathy and empathy and mislabels compassion.
This swaps empathy and sympathy and mislabels compassion.
This mislabels all three terms.

questions.q: A designer says: 'Poor first-years, getting lost must be awful.' In the unit's terms, which word fits this statement?
options: Empathy
Compassion
Sympathy
Observation
questions.explain: The statement feels for first-years from a distance and neither describes what they experience nor commits to any action, which is sympathy.
why_wrong: Empathy would be shown by following first-years and describing what actually happens.
Compassion would include a decision to act, such as renumbering the signage.
No observation of the first-years is described.

questions.q: A designer says: 'I followed three first-years for a morning. The block numbering resets in each wing.' Then the team decides: 'So we are renumbering the wing signage this week.' Which options correctly label the two statements?
options: The first is sympathy, and the second is empathy
The first is compassion, and the second is sympathy
Both are sympathy, since neither involves feeling for the first-years
The first is empathy, and the second is compassion
questions.explain: Following users to understand their experience is empathy. Turning that understanding into a decision to act is compassion. The unit's line is that empathy produces design and compassion produces a change.
why_wrong: The first statement shows real understanding, not distance.
The order is reversed; action comes only in the second statement.
The first statement is based on observation, not feeling from a distance.

questions.q: Which line from the unit sums up the three words?
options: Pity produces charity, empathy produces design, and compassion produces a change
Sympathy produces design, empathy produces charity, and compassion produces research
Pity produces design, empathy produces a change, and compassion produces charity
Empathy, sympathy and compassion all produce the same result
questions.explain: The unit ends its comparison with this line, tying each word to what it produces in practice.
why_wrong: This misassigns the results.
This swaps design, change and charity.
The unit says the three differ in what they produce.

questions.q: Which chain does the unit give for moving from watching users to designing for them?
options: Design, observe, understand, empathise
Observe, understand, empathise, design
Empathise, design, test, observe
Understand, design, observe, empathise
questions.explain: The unit shows the chain Observe, Understand, Empathize, Design: designing comes after observing and empathising.
why_wrong: Design cannot come first in this chain.
This is not the unit's chain.
This puts design before observation.

questions.q: In the unit's 'You Are Not the User' idea, what is the trap?
options: Asking six users who are not like you
Testing a prototype before building it
Assuming you know what users want because you might be a user yourself
Writing a problem statement without a solution in it
questions.explain: The trap is letting your own experience become the whole sample. The discipline is to treat it as one hypothesis and check with people who are not you.
why_wrong: Checking with six other people is the discipline, not the trap.
Testing is not part of this trap.
A problem statement without a solution is good practice.

questions.q: A team member says, 'I'm a student too, so I know what students need. Let's skip the interviews.' Which response follows the unit?
options: Agree, since being a user makes you a reliable sample
Replace the interviews with a larger survey of the team's friends
Interview only people who share the team's hostel and routine
Treat your experience as one hypothesis and go and check with several people who are not you
questions.explain: The unit's discipline is 'I think I know. Let me go and check with six people who are not me.' Your experience becomes one hypothesis, not the sample.
why_wrong: That is exactly the trap the unit warns about.
Friends of the team are people much like the team, so they do not fix the sample problem.
A sample of people similar to the team repeats the same bias.

questions.q: How does the unit define computational empathy?
options: Applying empathy to software development by designing systems that understand and respond to human emotions and behaviour, often using AI
A programmer's ability to feel what a computer is doing
Measuring user emotions only with surveys
Replacing human interviews with chatbots
questions.explain: Computational empathy is empathy applied in software, with systems that understand and respond to human emotions and behaviour, often through AI.
why_wrong: The definition is about users' emotions, not about the computer.
It is not limited to surveys.
The unit does not describe replacing interviews.

questions.q: Which pairing of system and empathic behaviour is correct in the unit's table?
options: Spotify monitoring well-being
Netflix recommending to suit mood
Healthcare apps matching listening habits
Educational apps understanding user intent
questions.explain: The unit pairs ChatGPT with understanding user intent, Netflix with recommending to suit mood, Spotify with matching listening habits, healthcare apps with monitoring well-being and educational apps with adapting to performance.
why_wrong: Spotify is paired with matching listening habits.
Healthcare apps are paired with monitoring well-being.
Educational apps are paired with adapting to performance.

questions.q: What was the scale of the problem in the CoWIN case study?
options: Delivering food to a single city
Managing exam results for one university
Scheduling and certifying vaccinations for over a billion people
Booking trains for a state
questions.explain: During the COVID-19 pandemic India needed to schedule and certify vaccinations for over a billion people with varied digital literacy and connectivity.
why_wrong: The case is national-scale vaccination.
The case is not about exams.
The case is not about trains.

questions.q: What was the key empathy insight in the CoWIN case?
options: Everyone has a smartphone and fast internet
Citizens prefer to register in person only
Language differences can be ignored at scale
One rigid flow would exclude millions of people
questions.explain: Teams recognised huge diversity: smartphone and feature-phone users, urban and rural, many languages and abilities. One rigid flow would have excluded millions.
why_wrong: The case stresses diversity of devices and connectivity.
Assisted and self-service pathways both existed.
Many languages were a design consideration, not something to ignore.

questions.q: Which set of features was part of CoWIN's response to the diversity of users?
options: Multiple assisted pathways, a common backend with many front-ends, and QR-verifiable certificates
A single app-only pathway with one language
Paper certificates only, issued at hospitals
A closed system with no access for third parties
questions.explain: The response included self, helpdesk and on-site pathways, a common backend with many front-ends, QR-verifiable certificates and slot APIs opened to third parties.
why_wrong: A single pathway is what the unit says would have excluded millions.
The certificates were QR-verifiable, not paper only.
The slot APIs were opened to third parties.

questions.q: What lesson does the unit draw from CoWIN?
options: Designing for the most digitally skilled users first gives the best results
Designing for the least-connected user and offering assisted pathways made inclusion possible at scale
A common backend should be avoided because it limits front-end options
Inclusion at scale needs a single rigid process for everyone
questions.explain: The lesson is to design for the least-connected user, and assisted pathways made inclusion possible at scale.
why_wrong: The unit argues for the opposite, the least-connected user.
CoWIN used a common backend with many front-ends.
A single rigid process is what would have excluded millions.

questions.q: Which type of research focuses on understanding why and how?
options: Quantitative research
A/B testing
Qualitative research
Web analytics
questions.explain: Qualitative research is about why and how and uses interviews, observations and focus groups. Quantitative research measures what and how many, using surveys, analytics and A/B tests.
why_wrong: Quantitative research measures what and how many.
A/B testing is a quantitative method.
Analytics is a quantitative method.

questions.q: What sample sizes does the unit give for qualitative and quantitative research?
options: Qualitative: 100 or more; quantitative: 5 to 20
Both use 5 to 20 participants
Qualitative: 50 to 60; quantitative: 5 to 10
Qualitative: 5 to 20 participants; quantitative: 100 or more
questions.explain: Qualitative research uses small samples of 5 to 20 participants, and quantitative research uses large samples of 100 or more.
why_wrong: This swaps the two.
The two methods use very different sample sizes.
These are not the figures in the unit.

questions.q: Which sequence does the unit recommend for combining the two kinds of research?
options: Use qualitative research to discover insights, then quantitative research to validate them at scale
Use quantitative research to discover insights, then qualitative research to validate them at scale
Use only qualitative research throughout
Use quantitative research first and skip qualitative research
questions.explain: The unit calls them partners, not rivals: qualitative for discovering insights and quantitative for validating them at scale.
why_wrong: This reverses the order.
The unit presents them as partners, so both are used.
Quantitative research comes second, not instead.

questions.q: Classify these four findings: (1) why students skip morning classes, (2) how many users abandon a shopping cart, (3) frustrations with hostel facilities, (4) click rates between two button designs.
options: (1) quantitative, (2) qualitative, (3) quantitative, (4) qualitative
(1) qualitative, (2) quantitative, (3) qualitative, (4) quantitative
(1) qualitative, (2) qualitative, (3) quantitative, (4) quantitative
(1) quantitative, (2) quantitative, (3) qualitative, (4) qualitative
questions.explain: 'Why' and 'frustrations' point to qualitative research. 'How many' and click rates are numbers, so they are quantitative.
why_wrong: This swaps every classification.
Cart abandonment counts are numbers, and frustrations are qualitative.
'Why students skip classes' needs qualitative exploration, and click rates are quantitative.

questions.q: Which of these is a characteristic of quantitative research in the unit?
options: Small, purposive sampling and subjectivity
Exploratory nature and contextual understanding
Numeric data, large samples and precision through statistical analysis
In-depth data collection and iterative analysis
questions.explain: The unit lists objectivity, numeric data, large samples, generalisability, standardised collection and statistical analysis for quantitative research. The other options describe qualitative research.
why_wrong: Small purposive sampling is qualitative.
Exploratory and contextual are qualitative traits.
In-depth collection and iterative analysis are qualitative traits.

questions.q: What does the unit say user research reduces?
options: The need for any prototype
The number of users to study
The cost of every project
Assumptions, by supporting evidence-based design decisions
questions.explain: User research answers who the users are, what problems they face, what they expect and what motivates them, which reduces assumptions.
why_wrong: Research does not remove the need to prototype.
It is about understanding users, not reducing their number.
The unit does not claim it reduces all costs.

questions.q: How does the unit define field observation?
options: Observing users in their natural environments, noting what they actually do rather than asking what they do
Asking users in a formal interview what they do
Measuring how many users click a button
Observing users only in a laboratory
questions.explain: Field observation means watching users in their natural environment. 'Be a fly on the wall' means do not interrupt or influence behaviour, and take notes discreetly.
why_wrong: That is an interview, not field observation.
That is quantitative analytics.
Field observation takes place in the natural environment.

questions.q: In the AEIOU framework, which letter stands for what people use during an activity, such as phones, laptops, books and applications?
options: A, for Activities
O, for Objects
E, for Environment
I, for Interactions
questions.explain: AEIOU stands for Activities, Environment, Interactions, Objects and Users. Objects are the tools, devices and products used during activities.
why_wrong: Activities are the tasks users perform.
Environment is the space where the activities happen.
Interactions are how users engage with people, products or systems.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the environmental factors the unit lists?
options: Interaction
Persona
Noise
Motivation
questions.explain: The unit lists lighting, noise, temperature, space and technology as key environmental factors.
why_wrong: Interaction is a separate AEIOU letter, not an environmental factor.
Persona is a research summary tool.
Motivation belongs to the Why stage of What-How-Why.

questions.q: A researcher notes at a photocopy shop: 'The operator asks "colour or black?" every single time, and the rate card does not answer it.' Which AEIOU letter does this belong to?
options: A, for Activities
O, for Objects
U, for Users
I, for Interactions
questions.explain: How the operator and customers engage, here a repeated question the rate card fails to answer, is an interaction between users and a system.
why_wrong: Activities are the steps users perform, such as queueing and paying.
Objects are the items used, such as pen drives and a cash tin.
Users describes who the people are.

questions.q: In the photocopy shop example, which note belongs under E, for Environment?
options: A single counter, one printer, no seating, a loud fan and a handwritten rate card taped at knee height
Four of eleven people left without printing after asking the price
Pen drives, phones, a Windows PC, a cash tin and a spiral-bound register
Mostly first- and second-years, arriving alone between classes
questions.explain: The setting itself, its layout, noise and signage, is the environment. People leaving is an activity, the devices are objects and the first- and second-years are users.
why_wrong: People leaving without printing is an activity.
Devices and a register are objects.
The first- and second-years describe the users.

questions.q: Which of these field notes is an observation and not a judgement?
options: The shop is badly managed
Four of eleven people left without printing after asking the price
Students are impatient
The operator does not care about customers
questions.explain: An observation records what happened and can be counted. 'Badly managed', 'impatient' and 'does not care' are judgements the observer has added.
why_wrong: The unit names this as a judgement, not an observation.
The unit names this as a judgement, not an observation.
This attributes motive to the operator, which is a judgement.

questions.q: What does the unit's rule 'Be a fly on the wall' mean?
options: Interview every person who walks past
Photograph people so you can study them later
Do not interrupt or influence behaviour, and take notes discreetly
Ask users to describe what they usually do
questions.explain: Field observation relies on seeing what people do without changing it. Interrupting, photographing people and asking them to describe it all alter or replace observed behaviour.
why_wrong: Interviewing is a different method and it interrupts.
The unit says not to photograph people.
Asking is not observing.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the research ethics rules in the unit?
options: Record people by their full names so the data is accurate
Photograph people to capture their expressions
Meet interviewees in private rooms for confidentiality
Ask first: never interview or photograph a person without clear permission
questions.explain: The unit's rules are ask first, say who you are, stay anonymous, do not photograph people and be safe. Use pseudonyms or initials, sketch scenes instead of photographing people, and meet in open public areas.
why_wrong: The unit says to use a pseudonym or initials.
The unit says do not photograph people and sketch the scene instead.
The unit says to meet in open, public campus areas.

questions.q: According to the unit, how should you record the people you interview?
options: By pseudonym or initials, never by full name
By full name and registration number
By their hostel room number
By a photograph attached to the notes
questions.explain: Staying anonymous is one of the rules: record people by pseudonym or initials.
why_wrong: Full names break the anonymity rule.
Room numbers identify people, and hostel rooms are residential spaces to avoid.
The unit says not to photograph people.

questions.q: Which of these is a suitable place to observe or interview, according to the unit?
options: A hostel room
A library reading area, a corridor, a bus stop or the mess seating area
A private office after dark
A person's home
questions.explain: The unit recommends public, appropriate places and says to avoid residential spaces such as hostel rooms. If in doubt, ask your faculty mentor.
why_wrong: The unit says to avoid residential spaces such as hostel rooms.
The unit asks for open, public areas in daylight.
A home is a private, residential space.

questions.q: A student wants to photograph a classmate using the photocopier for her observation notes. What does the unit advise?
options: Photograph discreetly, since photocopier shops are public
Photograph only if the person's face is hidden
Do not photograph people; sketch the scene instead and ask permission before studying an individual
Photograph and delete the picture after writing the notes
questions.explain: The unit says not to photograph people, to sketch instead, and to get consent before studying an individual. Observing public activity is fine, but studying an individual is not unless they agree.
why_wrong: The unit says not to photograph people even in public places.
The rule is not to photograph people; it does not allow face-hiding workarounds.
Deleting afterwards does not make taking the picture acceptable.

questions.q: Which of these is part of the verbal consent script?
options: That the interview will be recorded and shared with the college
That the person must answer every question
That the person's name and room will be used in the report
That it will take about five minutes, is voluntary, can be stopped or skipped at any time, and that no name will be recorded
questions.explain: The script says it will take about five minutes, it is completely voluntary, the person can stop or skip any question at any time, and the name will not be recorded.
why_wrong: The script promises no name is recorded and says nothing about sharing.
The script says the person can skip any question.
The script says no name is recorded.

questions.q: In the What-How-Why framework, which stage records what the user is doing, objectively?
options: What
How
Why
Who
questions.explain: What records actions and events objectively. How looks at how the task is performed, and Why uncovers motivations and emotions.
why_wrong: How analyses how the user performs the activity.
Why identifies motivations, emotions and needs.
Who is not one of the three stages.

questions.q: In a food delivery app study, which observation belongs in the WHAT stage?
options: The user scrolls back and forth, re-reading the delivery fees
The user opens the app, browses the menu and adds items to the cart
The user wants the best value for money
The user feels unsure about the final choice
questions.explain: What records the actions and events, such as opening the app and adding items. Scrolling back and forth is a how observation, and value for money and unsure feelings are why inferences.
why_wrong: Scrolling and re-reading show how the task is performed.
Wanting value for money is a motivation, which belongs to why.
Feeling unsure is an emotion, which belongs to why.

questions.q: In the same study, the user looks for promotions and re-reads the delivery fees. Which stage does this belong to?
options: What
Why
How
None; it is not an observation
questions.explain: How looks at how users complete tasks through their actions, effort, emotions and challenges, so re-reading fees and looking for promotions show how the task is performed.
why_wrong: What would list the plain actions, such as opening the app.
Why would infer motivations, such as wanting value for money.
It is an observable behaviour and so it belongs to How.

questions.q: 'The user wants the best value for money and is concerned about delivery fees.' In the unit's framework, what kind of note is this?
options: A What observation, since it is stated plainly
A How observation about effort
A fact that needs no evidence
A Why inference, which should be labelled as inference
questions.explain: Why is where motivations, emotions and needs are inferred, and the unit says this is where inference, carefully labelled as inference, begins.
why_wrong: Motivations cannot be directly observed, so they are not What notes.
How records actions and effort, not the motivation behind them.
An inference still needs to be marked as inference and supported by evidence.

questions.q: Which line does the unit use to summarise the relationship between observation and interpretation?
options: Observation without interpretation is data; interpretation without observation is guesswork
Interpretation without observation is data; observation without interpretation is guesswork
Observation and interpretation should never be combined
Interpretation is more reliable than observation
questions.explain: The unit pairs the two: observation alone is just data, and interpretation without observation is guesswork. Good work needs both, in order.
why_wrong: This reverses the line.
The framework moves from What and How to Why, so they are combined.
The unit does not rank interpretation above observation.

questions.q: Which of these is a characteristic of a good interview question, according to the unit?
options: Answerable with a simple yes or no
Open-ended, non-leading and about the user's own experience
Suggests the answer the interviewer expects
Asks the user to speculate about a future product
questions.explain: Good questions are open-ended, non-leading, exploratory and user-focused, about experiences and not hypotheticals.
why_wrong: Yes/no questions are closed.
That is a leading question.
Speculating about the future is a hypothetical.

questions.q: Which is the better version of 'Do you like the library?' in the unit's table?
options: Don't you think the library is too crowded?
Would you use a bigger library?
Tell me about your experience using the library
How much would you pay for a better library?
questions.explain: The better question is open-ended and invites a story about the person's experience. The other options are leading, hypothetical or about price.
why_wrong: This is leading, because it suggests an answer.
This is hypothetical and closed.
This is hypothetical.

questions.q: What does the 80/20 rule in interviews mean?
options: Talk 80 percent of the time to keep the interview moving
Ask 80 questions in a 20-minute interview
Spend 80 percent of the project on interviews
Listen more than you talk, and do not defend or explain your ideas
questions.explain: The unit says to listen more than you talk, which is the 80/20 rule, and not to defend or explain your own ideas.
why_wrong: That reverses the rule.
The rule is about talking and listening, not the number of questions.
The rule is about talk time within an interview.

questions.q: Which interview question breaks the rules because it is a hypothetical rather than about the person's real experience?
options: How much would you pay for a laundry service?
Tell me about the last time you did your laundry
Walk me through your typical Sunday evening in the hostel
What is frustrating about how you handle it now?
questions.explain: 'How much would you pay?' asks the user to speculate. The other three ask for a specific past episode, a walk-through or current frustrations.
why_wrong: This asks for a specific past episode, which is encouraged.
This is the grand tour technique.
This asks about current experience.

questions.q: Which question is leading, because it suggests the answer the interviewer expects?
options: How do you connect to the internet during a typical day?
Most students say the Wi-Fi is bad. Do you agree?
