Tell me about the last time the Wi-Fi caused you trouble
What do you do when the connection drops?
questions.explain: Telling the person what most others say and asking them to agree pushes them toward an answer. The other three ask open questions about the person's own experience.
why_wrong: This is an open question.
This asks for a specific past episode.
This asks about their own behaviour.

questions.q: Which interviewing technique does the unit call the hardest and the most productive?
options: The five whys
Grand tour
Embracing silence: wait three to five seconds and let people fill it
Show me
questions.explain: Embracing silence means waiting three to five seconds, because people fill silence with what they were not going to say.
why_wrong: The five whys is the first technique but is not called the hardest.
Grand tour is technique seven.
Show me is technique three.

questions.q: In the 'seek contradictions' interviewing technique, how should you raise a contradiction?
options: Directly, by telling the person they are wrong
By ignoring it to keep the interview smooth
By asking someone else to confirm which statement is true
Curiously, never accusingly, for example 'Earlier you said X, and just now Y'
questions.explain: The unit says to seek contradictions curiously and not accusingly, as in 'Earlier you said X, and just now Y'.
why_wrong: Accusing the person would damage the interview.
Contradictions are valuable because they reveal gaps between belief and behaviour.
The point is to explore it with the same person.

questions.q: In a Five Whys ladder, a student says 'I don't use the library much', then 'It's too crowded', then 'I can't concentrate with noise around me'. What does the unit say about the first Why?
options: It is almost never the real one
It is always the real cause
It is the only one worth recording
It should be accepted so as not to lead the interviewee
questions.explain: The unit says the first Why is almost never the real one and that you should keep peeling back layers until you reach a cause you can design for.
why_wrong: The unit says the opposite.
The whole ladder is recorded, and the deeper answers matter more.
Asking follow-up Whys is part of the technique and is not leading.

questions.q: In the unit's Five Whys example, the team started with 'build a bigger library'. Where did the ladder end?
options: 'Students need a quieter reading room'
'Students need a way to feel their study time is well spent'
'The library needs more books'
'Students need cheaper printing'
questions.explain: The ladder moved from a surface complaint through noise and exam pressure to a system that tests memorisation, and ended at the emotional core: students feel they are wasting time memorising instead of learning.
why_wrong: Noise was an early step, not the end of the ladder.
Books are not part of the example.
Printing is not part of the example.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: What are explicit needs, according to the unit?
options: What users actually need but never say
What the designer assumes users want
What observation reveals without any talking
What users say they want, stated clearly in interviews
questions.explain: Explicit needs are what users say they want, for example 'I want faster checkout'. Implicit needs are the unspoken ones revealed through observation and analysis.
why_wrong: That describes implicit needs.
Assumptions are what research is meant to replace.
That describes how implicit needs are discovered.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: A user says 'I want more features'. In the unit's table, which implicit need sits behind this explicit request?
options: A need for simplicity and guidance
A need for a faster app
A need for a lower price
A need for a bigger screen
questions.explain: The unit pairs 'I want more features' with a need for simplicity and guidance, and 'I want faster checkout' with a need to feel in control of the process.
why_wrong: Faster app is an explicit-need example.
Lower cost is an explicit-need example.
Screen size is not mentioned.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: Which of these is the unit's example of an implicit need?
options: Faster internet
Trust
Better battery
Lower cost
questions.explain: Safety, confidence, comfort, emotional support and trust are the unit's implicit-need examples. Faster internet, better battery, lower cost and a faster app are explicit.
why_wrong: Faster internet is an explicit-need example.
Better battery is an explicit-need example.
Lower cost is an explicit-need example.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: What does the unit say about the most innovative solutions?
options: They always respond only to explicit requests
They avoid user research altogether
They often address implicit needs that users could not articulate themselves
They copy the most common user complaint
questions.explain: The unit says the most innovative solutions often address implicit needs users could not put into words.
why_wrong: Explicit requests are already stated and produce expected solutions.
Research is how implicit needs are discovered.
Copying complaints leads to the obvious solution.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: What is the 'say-do gap'?
options: The gap between qualitative and quantitative research
The delay between a user's request and the product launch
The difference between a persona and an archetype
The gap between what people report and what they actually do
questions.explain: Designers call the gap between what people report and what they do the say-do gap. In the unit's coffee example, shoppers said they preferred a lighter roast but most reached for the dark one when offered a free cup.
why_wrong: This is not about research methods.
This is not about time delays.
This is not about personas.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: What rule does the unit give to deal with the say-do gap?
options: Ask what people do, and watch what people choose
Trust what people say, since they know best
Ignore stated preferences completely
Use only large surveys
questions.explain: The unit says stated preference is evidence about self-image and observed behaviour is evidence about need, so ask about doing and watch the choices.
why_wrong: The say-do gap shows that statements alone can mislead.
Stated preferences are still evidence, but about self-image.
Surveys also record what people say, so they carry the same risk.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: In the unit's coffee example, shoppers said they preferred a lighter roast, but when offered a free cup most reached for the dark. What does this show?
options: Shoppers lied deliberately to the researcher
Stated preference is evidence about self-image, and observed behaviour is evidence about need
Light roast is better than dark roast
Free items always change what people choose
questions.explain: The example illustrates the say-do gap. What people say reflects how they see themselves, and what they choose reveals what they actually need.
why_wrong: The unit does not suggest deliberate lying, only a gap between report and action.
The example is not about which roast is better.
The unit makes no claim about free items in general.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: Asked about a college app, a student says the timetable section is fine. Over a week, the researcher watches her screenshot the timetable every morning. What is the best reading?
options: A confirmed explicit need for screenshots
Proof that the timetable section needs no change
A possible implicit need, because what she does differs from what she says
Evidence that observations are less reliable than interviews
questions.explain: Saying 'fine' while screenshotting daily is a say-do gap and may point to an implicit need, such as wanting the timetable available instantly or offline.
why_wrong: She never asked for screenshots, so it is not an explicit request.
Her behaviour suggests it is not simply fine.
The unit holds that observed behaviour is evidence about need.

questions.q: How does the unit define pain points?
options: The features users ask for most often
The costs a company faces
The number of complaints in a year
Specific problems or frustrations users experience when trying to accomplish a goal
questions.explain: Pain points are specific problems or frustrations when users try to accomplish a goal. They fall into process, support, financial and productivity types.
why_wrong: Features requested are explicit needs, not pain points.
Company costs are not user pain points.
A count of complaints is evidence, not the definition.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four pain-point types named in the unit?
options: Aesthetic
Process
Support
Financial
questions.explain: The four types are process, support, financial and productivity. Productivity is the one that wastes time or effort.
why_wrong: Process pain points are inefficient or frustrating procedures.
Support pain points are a lack of help or guidance.
Financial pain points are costing too much money or time.

questions.q: A hosteller says: 'There is nobody to ask when the mess card fails at the counter.' Which pain-point type is this?
options: Process
Support
Financial
Productivity
questions.explain: A lack of help or guidance when something goes wrong is a support pain point.
why_wrong: Process pain points are about an inefficient procedure.
Financial pain points are about money or time cost.
Productivity pain points are about wasting time or effort.

questions.q: What does the unit say every recorded pain point needs?
options: A proposed solution
An approval from a mentor
Evidence, such as a quote or a count
A matching persona
questions.explain: Every pain point needs evidence, a quote or a count, so the team can see which ones have the weakest support and go and find out more.
why_wrong: A pain point is recorded before solutions are proposed.
Approval is not what the unit asks for.
Personas come from the research, not before it.

questions.q: Whom did Namma Yatri begin by studying?
options: Only the riders
The app's investors
Taxi company managers
The auto-rickshaw drivers, not just the riders
questions.explain: Most design attention in ride-hailing went to the rider. Namma Yatri, launched in Bengaluru with an auto-rickshaw drivers' union, began by studying the driver.
why_wrong: The case is about studying the other side of the app.
Investors are not part of the case.
Managers are not part of the case.

questions.q: According to the unit, what was the deepest pain point in the Namma Yatri case?
options: Powerlessness, not price
The price of fuel
Slow app loading
Too few riders
questions.explain: Drivers faced commission cuts, surge pricing that benefited the platform, unannounced algorithm changes and no route of appeal. The unit says the deepest pain point was powerlessness, not price.
why_wrong: Fuel price is not the finding.
App speed is not part of the case.
Ridership is not the issue raised.

questions.q: Which of these completes the Namma Yatri define statement?
options: Auto drivers need a mobile app, because customers want faster rides
Auto drivers need predictable, dignified incomes, because commission structures and opaque algorithms undermine both their earnings and their sense of control
Riders need cheaper fares, because surge pricing is unfair
The company needs more drivers, because demand is rising
questions.explain: The statement names the user (auto drivers), a need (predictable, dignified incomes) and an insight (commissions and opaque algorithms undermine earnings and control).
why_wrong: This bakes the solution (an app) into the statement.
This frames the problem around riders, not the driver studied.
This frames the problem around the company.

questions.q: What is the transferable lesson of the Namma Yatri case?
options: Zero-commission models work for every business
Riders should be ignored in ride-hailing design
Empathising with the person providing the service, not only the consumer, can produce radically different solutions
Open technology is always cheaper than closed technology
questions.explain: The unit's lesson is about whom you empathise with: studying the person who provides the service produced a very different model, a zero-commission pilot with a small subscription on open protocols.
why_wrong: The unit does not generalise the model to every business.
The lesson is to add the driver's side, not to ignore riders.
The unit makes no cost claim about open technology.

questions.q: In the Namma Yatri case, which of these was among the 'wild questions' that followed the empathy work?
options: What if riders paid double during peak hours?
What if the company hid its algorithm updates?
What if drivers were replaced by a fully automated service?
What if drivers paid a small flat subscription instead of a cut of every fare?
questions.explain: The wild questions included drivers owning the platform, no commission at all, a flat subscription and open technology so no single company controls it.
why_wrong: Higher peak pricing is the problem drivers described, not a question asked.
Opaque algorithm changes were a pain point.
Replacing drivers is not part of the case.

questions.q: How does the unit define a persona?
options: A fictional representation of a target user, based on real research data
A real customer's full profile
A guess about what users probably like
A list of product features
questions.explain: A persona is a fictional but research-based user. The unit calls it a research summary, not a character you invented.
why_wrong: Personas are fictional and anonymous.
Personas must be based on research, not guesses.
Personas describe users, not features.

questions.q: Which of these is a component of a persona listed in the unit?
options: The team's preferred solution
A representative quote from a real interview
A competitor's price list
The interviewer's opinion of the user
questions.explain: Persona components include a name, demographics, goals, frustrations, needs, behaviours and a representative quote, which must be real.
why_wrong: A persona describes the user, not the solution.
A competitor's prices are not a persona component.
Opinions of the interviewer are not part of a persona.

questions.q: Which persona line should be deleted, according to the unit's discipline that every line must trace to research?
options: 'I want to learn better and score good grades', from Interview 2 with pseudonym R
'Goal: score good grades', from several interviews
'Rahul loves cricket and drinks three coffees a day', when nobody said this
'Challenge: online lectures are hard to follow', as observed in two sessions
questions.explain: The unit's rule is: if you cannot point to the interview it came from, delete it. The cricket and coffee line is decoration, while the others trace to real interviews or observations.
why_wrong: This quote traces to a named interview.
This goal traces to the research.
This challenge traces to observations.

questions.q: How does the unit distinguish a persona from an archetype?
options: A persona is a broad group of users, and an archetype is one fictional individual
Both mean exactly the same thing
A persona is based on research, and an archetype is based on the designer's imagination
A persona is one fictional individual that helps the team empathise, and an archetype is a broad group with shared behaviour that helps the team segment
questions.explain: Archetypes are groups with similar behaviours, characteristics and needs, such as college students or senior citizens. A persona makes one such group concrete enough to design for.
why_wrong: This reverses the two.
The unit separates them clearly.
Both are based on research.

questions.q: What are the four quadrants of the empathy map in this unit?
options: Says, thinks, does and feels
Sees, hears, smells and tastes
Goals, challenges, needs and quotes
Activities, environment, interactions and users
questions.explain: The empathy map synthesises what users say, think, do and feel.
why_wrong: Those are senses, not empathy-map quadrants.
Those are persona components.
Those are four of the five AEIOU letters.

questions.q: On an empathy map, where should the evidence 'Rewatches the same lecture three times' go?
options: Says
Does
Thinks
Feels
questions.explain: An observable action belongs in Does. Says holds direct quotes, Thinks holds beliefs and concerns, and Feels holds emotions and attitudes.
why_wrong: Says holds direct quotes.
Thinks holds beliefs and concerns.
Feels holds emotions and attitudes.

questions.q: On an empathy map, where should 'Stressed before exams' go?
options: Says
Does
Feels
Thinks
questions.explain: Stress is an emotion, so it belongs in Feels.
why_wrong: Says holds direct quotes.
Does holds observable actions.
Thinks holds beliefs and concerns, such as 'Will I finish this course on time?'.

questions.q: A student's empathy map says 'The app is easy to use' while she rewatches the same lecture three times. What does the unit call this, and why does it matter?
options: A data error that should be removed
A sign she is lying, so the interview should be discarded
A normal pattern that needs no follow-up
A gap between Says and Does, which is usually the best opportunity
questions.explain: The unit says where Says and Does disagree is usually your best opportunity, since it points to a need the user cannot or does not state.
why_wrong: The unit treats the gap as insight, not as an error.
The unit treats it as something to explore, not as lying.
The unit treats it as worth following up.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: Which format does the unit give for a problem statement?
options: [User] needs [need] because [insight]
We need [solution] to fix [problem]
How might we [action] for [user]?
[User] wants [feature] so that [company] earns more
questions.explain: The unit's format has a user, a need and an insight. 'How might we' is a separate reframing tool.
why_wrong: This bakes the solution into the statement.
That is the How Might We format, a different tool.
This is not the unit's format.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: Why is 'We need a mobile app' a poor problem statement?
options: It is too long
It has no user, no need and no insight, and the solution is already baked in
It names too many users
It does not mention any technology
questions.explain: The unit labels it poor because it names no user, need or insight, and it assumes the solution.
why_wrong: It is short, not long.
It names no user at all.
It names a technology, which is part of the problem.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: Which is the unit's example of a good problem statement?
options: We need a campus navigation app
Students should get a map when they arrive
First-year students need a simple way to navigate campus because they frequently get lost and feel anxious about being late to class
The college needs better signage
questions.explain: The good example names a user, a need and an insight, and does not name a solution. The other options state solutions.
why_wrong: This names the solution, an app.
This names the solution, a map.
This names the solution, signage, and gives no user or insight.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: What does a How Might We (HMW) question do, according to the unit?
options: Ranks ideas by cost
Records a user's exact quotes
Lists the objects used in an observation
Reframes a problem as an opportunity for creative solutions
questions.explain: HMW questions reframe problems as opportunities, for example 'How might we reduce waiting time in the cafeteria?'.
why_wrong: Ranking ideas is a screening activity.
Quotes belong on an empathy map.
Objects belong to AEIOU.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: What does the Goldilocks test say about the HMW 'How might we add a red button to the timetable screen?'
options: It is too narrow, because it smuggles the solution into the question
It is too broad, because it covers every screen
It is just right, because it is specific
It is invalid, because HMW questions must be broad
questions.explain: A good HMW is in the middle, a real human need with no solution attached. A red button is a solution, so the question is too narrow. 'How might we improve education?' is the too-broad example.
why_wrong: Too broad would be a question like 'improve education'.
A specific solution is exactly what makes it too narrow.
HMW questions should be neither too broad nor too narrow.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: Which HMW passes the Goldilocks test?
options: How might we improve education?
How might we help new students find their classrooms without feeling anxious?
How might we add a map screen to the app?
How might we ask students to buy a navigation app?
questions.explain: The passing question names a real human need and attaches no solution. 'Improve education' is too broad, and the other two embed solutions.
why_wrong: This is the unit's too-broad example.
A map screen is a solution embedded in the question.
This embeds a particular product as the solution.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: In the Unit 2 capstone, what is the order of the pipeline?
options: Frame the problem, observe, interview, build a persona, then dig with five whys
Build a persona, observe, frame the problem, interview, then separate needs
Observe, interview, dig with five whys, separate explicit from implicit needs, build a persona and empathy map, then frame the problem
Interview, frame the problem, observe, build an empathy map, then dig with five whys
questions.explain: The capstone runs six steps: observe with an AEIOU scan, interview with consent, dig with one Five Whys ladder, separate two explicit and two implicit needs, build a persona and empathy map, and finally write the problem statement and an HMW.
why_wrong: Framing comes last, after the research.
A persona is built after the research, not before observation.
Framing the problem cannot come before observing and interviewing.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: Which two course outcomes does Unit 2 carry?
options: CO1 and CO2
CO1 and CO3
CO3 and CO4
CO2 (apply qualitative research and field observation to identify user requirements) and CO3 (analyse unstructured user data to formulate actionable design-challenge frameworks)
questions.explain: Unit 2 carries CO2 and CO3. CO1 is the Unit 1 outcome about human-centred design frameworks.
why_wrong: CO1 belongs to Unit 1.
CO1 belongs to Unit 1, and Unit 2 carries CO3 with CO2.
Unit 2 does not carry CO4.

questions.q: A team says: 'I'm a student too, so I know what students need. Let's skip the interviews.' Which response follows the unit?
options: Trust your own experience, since users are a sample of you, on that reading
Survey only your close friends, since they share your routine, as described
Interview only your hostel block, since you live there, taken at face value
Treat your experience as one hypothesis and check with others, in this case
questions.explain: The unit's discipline is to check with people who are not you, so your experience is one hypothesis and not the whole sample.
why_wrong: That is the trap the unit calls 'You Are Not the User'.
Friends who share your routine repeat the same bias.
One hostel block repeats the same narrow sample.

questions.q: Which pairing of system and empathic behaviour matches the unit's table?
options: Netflix monitors a user's well-being over time, given the scenario
ChatGPT recommends titles to suit the viewer's mood, for this team
Spotify matches its listening habits to the listener, in this case
Educational apps match songs to each learner's taste, as described
questions.explain: The unit pairs ChatGPT with understanding user intent, Netflix with recommending to suit mood, Spotify with matching listening habits, healthcare apps with monitoring well-being and educational apps with adapting to performance.
why_wrong: Netflix recommends to suit mood; healthcare apps monitor well-being.
ChatGPT is paired with understanding intent; Netflix recommends to suit mood.
Educational apps adapt to performance.

questions.q: Which CoWIN design choice shows 'design for the least-connected user'?
options: One app-only flow with a single language, on the basis of the details
Assisted pathways: self-service, helpdesk and on-site options, in all
Paper certificates only, issued at hospitals, on the details provided
A closed backend with no access for third parties, on the facts given
questions.explain: CoWIN offered self, helpdesk and on-site pathways, a common backend with many front-ends, QR-verifiable certificates and slot APIs opened to third parties.
why_wrong: One rigid flow would have excluded millions.
Certificates were QR-verifiable, not paper only.
Slot APIs were opened to third parties.

questions.q: A survey shows 38 of 50 day scholars reach their first lecture late each week. The team needs to know why. Which method fits?
options: Qualitative interviews and observation, since the need is why, on that reading
Another survey of five hundred students, since numbers settle it, as described
An A/B test of two timetable layouts, since testing shows causes, in this case
Web analytics on the college app, since logs record motives, in this situation
questions.explain: Qualitative research explores why and how with small samples. The survey has already measured how many; the missing piece is understanding.
why_wrong: More numbers would still say how many, not why.
An A/B test compares designs; it does not explain motives.
Analytics count behaviour, not reasons.

questions.q: Which plan follows the unit's sequence for combining research methods?
options: A survey of two hundred to find insights, then eight interviews to measure them, overall
Only interviews, because quantitative research is a rival method, from the details given
Only surveys, because interviews cannot be generalised at all, when all is said and done
Eight interviews to find insights, then a survey of two hundred to validate them, in all
questions.explain: Use qualitative research to discover insights, then quantitative research to validate them at scale. They are partners, not rivals.
why_wrong: That reverses the order.
The unit calls them partners, not rivals.
The unit uses both, in sequence.

questions.q: A researcher notes that the rate card is handwritten and taped at knee height. Which AEIOU letter holds this note?
options: A, the Activities, since it describes what people do, in practice
I, the Interactions, since it describes how users engage, overall
E, the Environment, since it describes the setting itself, in all
U, the Users, since it describes who the customers are, in effect
questions.explain: Environment covers the physical or digital space: layout, noise, lighting and signage. The rate card's placement is part of the setting.
why_wrong: Activities are the tasks users perform.
Interactions are how users engage with people or systems.
Users describes who the people are.

questions.q: At a photocopy shop the operator asks 'colour or black?' every single time, though a rate card hangs on the wall. Which AEIOU letter fits?
options: O, the Objects, since the rate card is a tool people use, in this situation
I, the Interactions, since it shows how users and the system engage, in all
E, the Environment, since the noise forces repeats, on the details provided
A, the Activities, since queueing and paying are the tasks noted, in effect
questions.explain: A repeated question the rate card fails to answer is an interaction between user and system, and it reveals a usability problem.
why_wrong: Objects are the tools used, such as pen drives and a cash tin.
Environment is the setting, such as noise and layout.
Activities are the tasks themselves, not how users engage.

questions.q: Which field note is an observation and not a judgement?
options: Four of eleven people left without printing after asking the price, in all
The shop is badly managed and the operator does not care, in this scenario
Students are impatient and will leave for any delay, all things considered
The operator is rude to customers at busy times, when all is said and done
questions.explain: An observation records what happened and can be counted. 'Badly managed', 'impatient' and 'rude' are judgements the observer added.
why_wrong: That is a judgement; the unit names 'badly managed' as one.
That is a judgement; the unit names 'impatient' as one.
That attributes behaviour and motive without evidence.

questions.q: A student wants to photograph a classmate using the photocopier for observation notes. What does the unit advise?
options: Photograph discreetly, since the shop is a public place, on that reading
Photograph only if the face is hidden from the frame, on the facts given
Photograph freely and delete the picture once the notes are done, in all
Do not photograph people; sketch the scene and ask first, as framed here
questions.explain: The unit says never to photograph people, to sketch scenes instead, and to get consent before studying an individual.
why_wrong: Public places still do not allow photographing people under the unit's rules.
The rule is not to photograph people at all.
Deleting afterwards does not make taking the picture acceptable.

questions.q: In a food delivery app study, the user scrolls back and forth and re-reads the delivery fees. Which stage is this?
options: What: it records the plain actions taken, on the facts given
Why: it reveals the user's motive and needs, on that reading
How: it shows the effort and challenge in the task, in short
None: observation notes cannot include effort at all, in all
questions.explain: How explores the way the task is done: actions, effort, emotions and challenges. What records plain actions, and Why infers motivations.
why_wrong: What lists plain actions such as opening the app.
Why infers motivation, such as wanting good value.
How notes do include effort and emotions.

questions.q: Which interview question breaks the rules by being a hypothetical?
options: Tell me about the last time you did your laundry, on that reading
How much would you pay for a laundry service, taken at face value
Walk me through your typical Sunday evening in the hostel, in all
What is frustrating about how you handle it now, in this scenario
questions.explain: Hypothetical questions ask people to speculate. The unit prefers specific past episodes, walk-throughs and current frustrations.
why_wrong: A specific past episode is encouraged.
A walk-through is the grand tour technique.
Asking about current experience is encouraged.

questions.q: In a Five Whys ladder a student says 'I don't use the library much', then 'It's too crowded'. What does the unit say about these early answers?
options: The first Why is almost never the real one, so keep asking, in effect
Accept 'too crowded' as the cause and design a bigger library, in all
Stop after two answers so the interview stays neutral, as framed here
Replace the questions with a survey about library size, for this team
questions.explain: The ladder moved from crowding to noise, to exam pressure, to a system that tests memorisation, ending at the emotional core. The first Why is almost never the real one.
why_wrong: A bigger library answers the symptom, not the cause.
Stopping early keeps the symptom as the answer.
A survey replaces the exploration the ladder is for.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: A user says 'I want more features'. In the unit's table, which implicit need sits behind it?
options: A need to feel in control of the process, in practice
A need for a faster app with a longer battery, in all
A need for a lower price and cheaper plans, in effect
A need for simplicity and guidance, in this situation
questions.explain: The unit pairs 'I want more features' with a need for simplicity and guidance, and 'I want faster checkout' with a need to feel in control.
why_wrong: Feeling in control pairs with 'faster checkout'.
Faster app and battery are explicit needs.
Lower cost is an explicit need.

questions.topic: Explicit and Implicit Needs, Say-Do Gap
questions.q: Shoppers said they preferred a lighter roast of coffee, but offered a free cup most reached for the dark. What does the unit conclude?
options: Shoppers lied on purpose, so interviews are useless, on the facts given
Light roast is simply better, so the free cup misled them, in this case
Stated preference shows self-image, and choices show need, as described
Free items always change what people choose, in every setting, in short
questions.explain: This is the say-do gap. What people say is evidence about self-image, and what they choose is evidence about need.
why_wrong: The unit does not say they lied on purpose.
The example is not about which roast is better.
The unit makes no claim about free items in general.

questions.q: A hosteller says 'There is nobody to ask when the mess card fails at the counter.' Which pain-point type is this?
options: Process, an inefficient or frustrating procedure, in all
Support, a lack of help or guidance, taken at face value
Financial, costing too much money, all things considered
Productivity, wasting time or energy, given the scenario
questions.explain: The four types are process, support, financial and productivity. A lack of help when something goes wrong is a support pain point.
why_wrong: Process pain points are about the procedure itself.
Financial pain points are about cost.
Productivity pain points are about wasted time or effort.

questions.q: What did Namma Yatri's research identify as the deepest pain point for auto drivers?
options: Powerlessness, with no appeal against algorithm changes, in all
High fuel prices that cut into their daily earnings, on balance
Slow app loading on older and cheaper phones, in this situation
Too few riders on the platform in off-peak hours, for this team
questions.explain: The unit says the deepest pain point was powerlessness, not price: commission cuts, surge pricing that benefited the platform, unannounced algorithm changes and no route of appeal.
why_wrong: Fuel prices are not mentioned in the case.
App speed is not part of the case.
Rider numbers are not the issue in the case.

questions.q: Which persona line should be deleted under the unit's rule that every line must trace to research?
options: 'I want to learn better and score good grades', from Interview 2, pseudonym R, in all
'Goal: score good grades', from several interviews, given all the details stated here
'Challenge: online lectures are hard to follow', seen in two sessions, as framed here
'Rahul loves cricket and drinks three coffees a day', which nobody said, in this case
questions.explain: A persona is a research summary. If you cannot point to the interview a line came from, delete it. The cricket and coffee line is decoration.
why_wrong: That quote traces to a named interview.
That goal traces to several interviews.
That challenge traces to observed sessions.

questions.q: On an empathy map, a student says 'The app is easy to use' but rewatches the same lecture three times. What does the unit say?
options: The gap is a data error, so the Says quadrant should be removed, in all
The gap proves she lied, so the interview should be discarded, in short
The Says and Does gap is usually the best opportunity, in this scenario
The gap is normal and needs no follow-up, with everything stated so far
questions.explain: Where Says and Does disagree is usually your best opportunity: it points to a need the user does not or cannot state.
why_wrong: The unit treats the gap as insight, not error.
The unit treats it as something to explore, not lying.
The unit says it deserves follow-up.

questions.topic: Problem Statements and How Might We
questions.q: Which How Might We question passes the Goldilocks test?
options: How might we improve education across the whole college, for this team
How might we help new students find classrooms without anxiety, in all
How might we add a map screen to the college app, based on the details
How might we make students install a navigation app, in this situation
questions.explain: A good HMW names a real human need and attaches no solution. 'Improve education' is too broad, and the other two embed solutions.
why_wrong: That is the unit's too-broad example.
A map screen is a solution inside the question.
A specific product is a solution inside the question.

questions.q: A designer says: 'I followed three first-years for a morning. The block numbering resets in each wing.' Which word fits this statement?
options: Empathy, since it understands the situation as they live it, in all
Sympathy, since it feels for them from a distance, in this scenario
Compassion, since it already includes a decision to act, on balance
Pity, since it voices concern without any research, on that reading
questions.explain: Empathy is understanding a situation as the user experiences it. Sympathy feels for someone at a distance, and compassion adds the decision to act.
why_wrong: Sympathy would be 'poor first-years, getting lost must be awful'.
The statement describes observation, not a decision to act.
Pity produces charity; this statement rests on real observation.
